analysis.one_liner: Bars bankruptcy courts from wiping out government claims against a bankrupt company's owners and executives.
analysis.headline: The bill died in a House Judiciary subcommittee without a single vote in committee or on the floor, despite 63 Democratic cosponsors and none from the other party.
analysis.plain_summary: When a company goes bankrupt, some courts have allowed the company's owners, officers, and directors — people who are not themselves bankrupt — to walk away from lawsuits as part of the bankruptcy deal. This bill would stop bankruptcy courts from releasing lawsuits brought by states, tribes, cities, or the federal government against those people, though a judge could pause such lawsuits for up to 90 days. It was written with the Purdue Pharma case in mind, where the family that owned the OxyContin maker sought legal immunity through the company's bankruptcy. The bill never received a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: State attorneys general, tribes, cities, and the federal government keeping the power to sue the wealthy owners and executives of bankrupt companies directly — and the victims of corporate wrongdoing whose claims those governments bring.
analysis.who_benefits_short: States, tribes, cities, and federal prosecutors

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits bankruptcy courts from releasing or blocking claims by a State, municipality, federally recognized Tribe, or the United States against a non-debtor — such as a bankrupt company's officers, directors, or owners — except as allowed under the existing asbestos trust provision of bankruptcy law.
Lets a bankruptcy court pause such lawsuits for at most 90 days, so a brief breathing room is allowed but a permanent shield is not.

The bill responds to a court split: some appeals courts allow bankruptcy plans to release non-debtors from liability and some do not, which until now left government claims against a bankrupt company's owners dependent on where the case was filed.

analysis.who_pays: Controlling shareholders, officers, and directors of companies in bankruptcy, and their insurers, who could no longer trade money for blanket immunity from government lawsuits through their company's bankruptcy case.
analysis.who_pays_short: Owners and executives of bankrupt companies

drawbacks.text: Bankruptcy practitioners argue non-debtor releases can be the glue that holds a mass-tort settlement together: creditors may not pay in unless the owners kick in money and get peace, so banning releases could leave victims with slower, riskier recoveries. The bill's 90-day cap on stays acknowledges this concern but does not allow a consensual deal to be court-locked in the same way.

The bill is narrower than the problem it names: it protects only claims brought by states, tribes, municipalities, or the federal government, leaving private claims by individual victims — including many of the opioid lawsuits filed by personal-injury plaintiffs — outside its protection.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For anyone who thinks wealthy company owners should not be able to buy immunity from government lawsuits through an entity they no longer need, the benefit clearly outweighs the cost: the bill preserves every bankruptcy protection for the company itself and touches only the owners' personal exposure to government claims. The genuine cost is practical — mass-tort settlements often lean on non-debtor releases to get money moving to victims, and this bill removes that tool for government-claim settlements — but the bill's authors judged that preserving public enforcement was worth it, and they left a 90-day stay as a pressure valve.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, later sent to a subcommittee, and never received a markup or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Carolyn Maloney introduced the SACKLER Act on March 19, 2021, joined by Rep. Mark DeSaulnier, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.

In October 2021 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Antitrust, Commercial, and Administrative Law, and the record shows no further action — no hearing or markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote.
The bill ended the 117th Congress with 63 cosponsors, all of them Democrats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wealthy owners and executives of bankrupt companies, and the restructuring industry, keep the ability to secure broad immunity from government lawsuits inside their company's bankruptcy; states and tribes must continue litigating those claims case by case.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Owners of bankrupt companies and the restructuring industry

sides.party_line_note: All 63 cosponsors were Democrats and the bill sat in a Democratically controlled committee, so both support and inaction ran along party lines.

industries.industry: Controlling owners and executives of companies in bankruptcy
industries.note: The bill would end their ability to use their company's bankruptcy to buy blanket immunity from state, tribal, local, and federal lawsuits, which matters most in mass-tort cases where the owners are richer than the company. Ordinary people — the victims whose claims these governments pursue — benefit when that shield is unavailable.

Non-debtor releases are a core settlement tool in large mass-tort bankruptcies; banning them for government claims removes leverage the restructuring industry uses to close deals. Some practitioners argue this slows compensation to victims, which is the industry's strongest public-facing argument.
